title: Der, Die, Das Exercises with Answers (A1)
rule: In Nominativ, use der for masculine nouns, die for feminine nouns and das for neuter nouns. Learn the article together with the noun, not as an afterthought.
trap: Do not guess an article from an English translation: German grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender.
quiz: Stuhl is masculine in the singular.
All plural nouns use die in Nominativ.

title: Ein or Eine? A1 Article Practice with Answers
rule: Use ein before a masculine or neuter singular noun in Nominativ, and eine before a feminine singular noun. There is no indefinite article for ordinary plural nouns.
trap: A singular feminine noun needs eine, even when the English sentence says only “a”.
quiz: The usual plural has no ein/eine article.

title: Kein or Keine? German A1 Negation Exercises
rule: Negate an indefinite noun phrase with kein in masculine/neuter Nominativ and keine in feminine or plural Nominativ. Other cases change the ending: keinen is masculine Akkusativ.
trap: Do not replace every nicht with kein: kein typically negates a noun phrase, not an adjective or verb.
quiz: Fehler is masculine Nominativ after sein.

title: Sein Conjugation Exercises for A1 Beginners
rule: The verb sein is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. Practise the whole sentence so you connect the subject to its form.
trap: Do not write ich ist or ihr sind; English am/is/are does not map word for word to German.

title: Haben Conjugation Practice (A1) with Answers
rule: Use habe with ich, hast with du, hat with er/sie/es, haben with wir and sie/Sie, and habt with ihr. Haben is also the helping verb in many Perfekt sentences.
trap: Keep habt for ihr; wir habt is incorrect.

title: German Regular Verb Endings: A1 Exercises
rule: In the present tense, regular verbs often take -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en for ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie. The verb stem remains recognizable.
trap: For stems ending in -t or -d, German may insert an extra e in forms such as du arbeitest.

title: Ich, Du, Er, Sie, Es: A1 Pronoun Exercises
rule: German subject pronouns identify who does an action: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie. Capital Sie is the formal “you”; lowercase sie can mean she or they.
trap: Do not confuse sie (she), sie (they) and Sie (formal you): context and verb ending help.
examples: Meine Mutter arbeitet. Sie ist Ärztin.
My mother works. She is a doctor.
Mein Bruder lernt. Er ist fleißig.
My brother studies. He is diligent.
Das Kind schläft. Es ist müde.
The child sleeps. It is tired.
quiz: Anna is represented by feminine singular sie.

title: Mein, Meine, Dein, Deine: A1 Practice
rule: Possessives behave like ein-words: mein Vater, meine Mutter, mein Kind, meine Freunde. The ending changes with gender, case and number, not with the speaker’s gender.
trap: The word mein does not always get -e just because the owner is female.

title: German W-Questions: A1 Fill-in-the-Blank Practice
rule: Use wer for a person, was for a thing, wo for location, wohin for destination, woher for origin, wann for time and warum for reason. In a direct question the conjugated verb usually comes next.
trap: Wo and wohin are different: one asks where someone is, the other where someone goes.
quiz: ___ ist das? — Das ist mein Lehrer.

title: German Yes/No Questions: Word Order Practice A1
rule: To form a yes/no question, place the conjugated verb first, then the subject: Kommst du? Hast du Zeit? Answer with ja, nein, or sometimes doch when contradicting a negative question.
trap: Do not keep the normal statement order when you turn it into a yes/no question.
quiz: The finite verb opens the question.
Use ihr → habt, before the subject.

title: Where Does Nicht Go? A1 German Practice
rule: Nicht negates a verb, adjective, adverb or particular part of a sentence. Its position depends on what is negated: Ich komme heute nicht; Das ist nicht teuer.
trap: Use kein to negate an indefinite noun phrase: Ich habe kein Auto, not Ich habe nicht Auto.
examples: She does not live in Berlin.
We do not understand the question.
quiz: An adjective can be negated with nicht.
Here the whole action is negated.
Here the place phrase is negated.
Geld is a neuter noun phrase; kein is natural here.

title: German Numbers and Prices: A1 Practice
rule: For numbers 21–99, German usually says the ones before the tens: einundzwanzig (21), fünfunddreißig (35). To say a price, use Euro and Cent naturally.
trap: Do not translate twenty-one word for word as zwanzigeins.
examples: Der Bus kommt in fünf Minuten.
The bus comes in five minutes.

title: German Time Expressions: A1 Uhrzeit Exercises
rule: Use um before a clock time: um acht Uhr. Informal halb neun means 8:30, because German names the next hour. Viertel nach acht is 8:15; Viertel vor neun is 8:45.
trap: Halb neun is not 9:30. Think of being halfway toward nine.
examples: Der Kurs beginnt um acht Uhr.
Wir treffen uns um Viertel vor sechs.
We meet at quarter to six.
quiz: Quarter to six in a twelve-hour expression.
The lesson is at 7:00 = Der Unterricht ist ___ sieben Uhr.
Use um before a clock time.

title: Akkusativ Articles Practice: Den, Die, Das at A1
rule: With a masculine direct object, der changes to den and ein changes to einen. Feminine die and neuter das stay unchanged in Akkusativ; plural die also stays die.
trap: Only the masculine article clearly changes in these definite-article examples. Do not turn every object into den.
